hearthstead.guide.attributes.body: Every settler is built from five numbers, 0 to 100: Strength (what they carry, and a blow's force), Stamina (how long a shift they stand), Wits (how fast they learn, and craft precision), Dexterity (fine work at fields, benches, looms) and Spirit (morale under pressure, and how much they lift those near them). A newcomer's five numbers are all capped at fifteen out of a hundred, so nobody arrives a hero — except in their one knack, a single attribute quietly rolled to lean toward that cap instead of away from it.
hearthstead.guide.attributes.body2: Attributes grow only by doing the work that trains them — a lumberer's axe builds Strength, a courier's rounds build Stamina. Growth is slow and never finishes: a settler trained for weeks is one you built. Wits speeds every attribute's growth, itself included, so schooling a clever settler early pays for life. Most settlers carry a trait, sometimes two, and every trait costs something: strong backs carry more and walk slower; quick studies learn faster, a step behind on everything else.
hearthstead.guide.attributes.title: Attributes
hearthstead.guide.dagsverk.body: Every settler carries a second, quieter number alongside their needs: Dagsverket, the work still in them today. A newcomer starts with twenty units and spends a little every time they finish something — felling a tree, harvesting a crop, closing a production batch, walking a patrol leg — never on a timer, only on work actually completed. Once it runs dry, that trade simply stops taking new work for the day, and whatever a settler already does when idle takes over; nobody needs telling to go rest.
hearthstead.guide.dagsverk.body2: Dagsverket refills at wake, not at midnight, and how much depends on where a settler slept: a real bed gives it back in full, a rough night by the hearth only three-fifths of it — a village of open-air sleepers is visibly less productive than one with real houses. Trained Stamina raises the ceiling itself, so a hardened settler simply gets more day than a green one. A guard's patrols draw on the same pool, though never their sword: answering an alarm or standing a fight costs nothing from it, however tired their legs already are.
hearthstead.guide.dagsverk.title: Dagsverk
hearthstead.guide.day.body: The whole settlement shares one clock. At Rise everyone wakes and the square fills; through Morning and Afternoon Work they walk to their trade — unless it is farmed or felled, where the work already is. At the midday Meal they gather in the dining hall, and come Evening the tavern and square fill again before Rest sends everyone to bed. A phase is a habit, never a law: a raid or real exhaustion overrides it. Guards keep half their number on a night watch, so someone is always walking.
hearthstead.guide.day.title: The Day
hearthstead.guide.founding.body: Craft a Hearth from logs, cobblestone and a campfire, then set it on open ground, well clear of any settlement already standing. The moment it catches, three settlers gather at the fire and your settlement is born — named, with a working radius around the hearth. Keep bread and other food in its stores: hungry settlers eat there, and a well-fed settlement draws travelers to join it. Break the hearth, and everything tied to it ends.
hearthstead.guide.founding.title: Founding
hearthstead.guide.jobs.body: Right-click a working building's plaque and open the Hire tab to see who could take the post. Every candidate is a card, not a number: pips show how well suited they are, and the card states plainly what taking them costs — nothing, or that their building would be left with nobody. Press Hire and they walk over, ten morale happier. Dismissing someone from the People tab is never free: they lose morale and stand idle rather than vanish, so every choice's cost stays in plain sight.
hearthstead.guide.jobs.title: Jobs
hearthstead.guide.logistics.body: Couriers keep goods moving: they lift crates from the hearth's stores — never food, which stays there for hungry settlers — and carry them to a warehouse, one bag-load at a time. What a courier carries is real and visible on her back, out of the hearth's stores and not yet the warehouse's. If she falls in a raid the load spills at her feet instead of vanishing. Chests are the truth throughout: nothing is ever tallied that is not sitting in a real container somewhere.
hearthstead.guide.logistics.title: Logistics
hearthstead.guide.mayor.body: One settler speaks for the whole settlement. Appoint a mayor and their knack decides what it grows good at — a strong mayor quickens every trade, a clever one speeds learning, a warm one steadies morale, and so for each of the five. A new mayor's gift takes a day and a half to show, so swapping ahead of a raid you can see coming works, but swapping every morning does not. Losing a mayor is a real blow: morale falls settlement-wide, and the seat sits empty three days before anyone may take it again.
hearthstead.guide.mayor.title: The Mayor
hearthstead.guide.plaque.body: A hung plaque starts blank and does nothing at all — no screen, no scan — until you fit a Build Plan into it. Craft a plan for the building you want and use it on the plaque: that stamps its purpose and sets it surveying the room around it. The plaque glows what it finds: dark while blank, red until something is met, amber once part of the room qualifies, green the moment all of it does.
hearthstead.guide.plaque.body2: Every building type wants different things — a house asks for a bed, a door and light; a smithy wants an anvil, a smithing table and a forge nearby. Right-click the plaque to read exactly what your room still needs, ticking off line by line. It re-checks itself every ten seconds on its own, or press Refresh in its own screen to see a change at once.
hearthstead.guide.plaque.title: The Plaque
hearthstead.guide.recruiting.body: A fed, well-morale settlement draws travelers on its own; a Tavern draws them faster, and a Tavern with an innkeeper working it faster still. An arriving guest walks to the tavern — or the hearth, if you have none yet — and simply waits; arriving is not joining. The price is four bread and eight planks of any wood, paid straight out of the hearth the instant it can be met. The village haggles for you: an innkeeper on shift and a standing dining hall each take a quarter off, never deeper than half. Patience is not endless — about two and a half days, doubled with an innkeeper, then they walk away.
hearthstead.guide.recruiting.title: Recruiting
hearthstead.guide.research.body: The Architect's Study — a lectern flanked by bookshelves — is where a settlement studies itself. Hire a scholar to work there and right-click the lectern to open Prøvebenken, the trial bench: choose one project, pay its cost in paper and a sample of the trade it studies, and the scholar advances it in steady stints at the lectern. An unattended study is not wasted — a small trickle of progress rolls in on its own — but a working scholar is always the real engine. Cancelling a project part-done returns half its sample, never the paper already spent.
hearthstead.guide.research.body2: Six projects are open from the start, each aimed at one part of the settlement's own work: better yeast for the bakery, seasoned timber for the sawmill, iron blestring for the smelter, tanning acid for the tannery, a crop rotation for the fields, and a drill regimen for the guard. Every one finishes into the same shape — a modest, permanent bonus to the work it studies, never a gate — so a settlement that never researches anything still runs, just a little slower than one that does.
hearthstead.guide.research.title: Research
hearthstead.guide.saga.body: Every raid captain who reaches your walls has a name, and one who gets away with what they came for earns a second — 'the Grain-Thief' for one who stole your harvest, 'Larder's Bane' for one who has done it more than once — each a claim you can check against the raid's own report. A captain remembers too: the settler who hurt them most becomes a grudge carried into the next fight, and cutting one down only passes it on — whoever answers next inherits both the grudge and a name sworn to the one who fell.
hearthstead.guide.saga.title: The Saga
hearthstead.guide.summons.body: Right-click a working building's plaque and press Summon to call whoever works there straight to their post — useful for a farmer sleeping off a bad night in the wrong field, or a guard who wandered off to watch instead of fight. A bell rings where you stood; the settler answers with a low murmur wherever they are, then starts walking, glowing the whole way through walls so you can watch them coming. A summons lasts about a minute and a half — past that they simply forget they were called, and the glow fades with it.
hearthstead.guide.summons.title: Summons
hearthstead.guide.threat.body: There is no safe night. Every night rolls its own chance of a raid, between five and fifty-five in a hundred, rather than counting down a fixed timer a player could learn and ignore. A settlement too small or too empty is left alone entirely; grow past that, and the world starts paying attention. Surviving a raid makes you a bigger target, not a safer one — pressure rises when you win, and only eases a little when you lose, because losing costs settlers, buildings and stores.
hearthstead.guide.threat.body2: How dangerous tonight is has a name, and it is never hidden: run /hearthstead info to read your settlement's stage — Rolig (calm), Uro (unease), Varsel (warning) or Beleiring (siege) — beside the raw pressure, tonight's exact chance, and nights since the last attack. One mercy holds at every stage but the worst: a raid never lands the night straight after another, so a settlement just hit always gets one clear night before the world comes calling again.
hearthstead.guide.threat.title: Threat
hearthstead.guide.title: Settler's Handbook
hearthstead.guide.watch.body: A guard's rank is not chosen, it is earned — read straight off the same Strength every guard trains by patrolling and fighting. A recruit carries only their sword; twenty points in makes a Spearman in a leather chestplate; forty makes a Veteran in full leather, whose swing now catches a second foe with Cleave; sixty makes a Sergeant, iron at chest and legs, able to Leap Strike into a knot of enemies at once; eighty makes a Captain, head to toe in iron.
hearthstead.guide.watch.body2: The kit is bought, not issued: a promotion takes real armour out of the armoury, and a guard who ranks up before the smith has delivered stands in cloth until it arrives. Patrolling trains Strength slowly; landing a blow in a real fight trains it five times as fast, because a veteran is evidence of nights survived, not drills attended. Whoever holds the highest rank is the settlement's captain, and it shows: an off-duty settler who passes them will stop, turn and murmur a greeting. The archer earns their own ranks the same way, off Dexterity, at the watchtower.
hearthstead.guide.watch.title: The Watch
